sources.entry: C/C++11 mappings to processors - The table that turns each memory order into x86 and Arm instructions, so what an order costs is read off the page.

summary.title: C/C++11 mappings to processors
summary.one_liner: A reference table showing the x86, Power, ARMv7, ARMv8 (AArch32/AArch64) and Itanium instruction sequences that each C/C++11 atomic memory order compiles to.
keywords: how much does memory order cost
takeaways: Each C/C++11 operation (relaxed, consume, acquire, release, seq_cst, fences, compare-exchange) is mapped to a concrete instruction sequence per architecture.
On x86, plain MOVs implement most orders; seq_cst stores need a LOCK XCHG or MOV plus MFENCE, and seq_cst fences use MFENCE.
ARMv8 LDAR/STLR can implement seq_cst operations directly, while ARMv7 and Power rely on dmb ish or hwsync/lwsync barriers around accesses.
The page warns that compilers must agree on one SC mapping (read-fencing vs write-fencing on x86, or the two ARM variants), otherwise linked code may be incorrect.
The mappings are per-operation, not optimised; redundant barriers between adjacent operations could be removed by an optimisation pass.
summary.summary: The page is a collection of known mappings from C/C++11 atomic operations to x86, PowerPC, ARMv7, ARMv8 (AArch32 and AArch64) and Itanium instruction sequences, offered for discussion rather than as a definitive source. Each architecture gets a table listing the instructions for loads, stores, compare-exchange and fences under each memory order. The author notes that the per-operation approach is simpler than barrier-between-operations tables (such as Doug Lea's JVM cookbook) and that no optimisations are covered. Sources cited include the Batty et al. POPL 2011/2012 papers and ARM barrier litmus test material.
